goals: Compare make-to-stock, make-to-order, assemble-to-order and engineer-to-order.
Explain how MRP turns a production plan into dated orders for parts.
Describe the four dimensions of quality in logistics.
Set quality KPIs: OTIF, order accuracy, lead time and the perfect order.
Measure customer satisfaction with surveys, complaint logs and NPS.
Improve processes with PDCA, the 8 Lean wastes, 5 Whys and the fishbone diagram.

handout.intro: The Make stage turns materials into products ready for customers. In logistics, quality means more than a good product: it means the whole delivery is right. This session shows how to plan production, measure quality and keep improving.

head: Strategy
How it works
Example
Stock and speed
rows: Keep parts ready; assemble when the order comes
A laptop with a chosen memory size
Start making only after the order
Design and make for one customer
A special crane for a port

blocks.p: The point where the customer’s order starts the work is called the **order penetration point** (or decoupling point). Before it, you work to the forecast; after it, you work to the order.

list: the **production plan** (what and when to make),
the **bill of materials (BOM)** (which parts each product needs),
**stock levels and lead times** for each part.

blocks.p: Example: you plan 500 bicycles for 1 May. Each needs 2 wheels → 1,000 wheels. You have 200 in stock, so you need 800. The supplier takes 3 weeks, so MRP says: **order 800 wheels by 10 April**.
A perfect product can still be a poor delivery. Logistics quality has four dimensions:

head: Dimension
Question
rows: Did the customer get exactly what they ordered: right items, right quantity?
Did it arrive in the agreed window?
Were the confirmation, tracking, labels and invoice all correct?
Was the driver helpful, the packaging good, and the problem solved quickly?

blocks.p: Quality in logistics is usually **invisible until it fails**. Customers notice the missing pallet, not the 99 perfect ones. So quality must be **built into the process**, not checked at the end.

head: KPI
How to calculate
Example
rows: Orders on time AND complete ÷ all orders × 100
Orders with no errors ÷ all orders × 100
Orders that are on time, complete, undamaged and with correct documents ÷ all orders

blocks.p: Set targets from **what the customer needs**: a hospital may need 99.5% OTIF; a fashion shop may accept 95%. Write exact definitions: is “on time” the time the truck **left** or the time the customer **received** the goods?

callout.title: Fewer, better KPIs
callout.text: Six well-chosen KPIs that people act on are better than thirty that nobody reads. Try the **OTIF** tool in Tools.

list: **Short surveys** soon after delivery (“Did the driver arrive in the window?”), with one open question.
**Complaint log** – record date, customer, problem, cause, time to fix. Look for patterns: 20 late-delivery complaints from one depot is a signal.
**Net Promoter Score (NPS)** – “How likely are you to recommend us?” (0–10). NPS = % promoters (9–10) − % detractors (0–6).

blocks.p: Measuring is useless without **action**. When customers see their feedback leads to change, they keep giving it.

steps: **Plan** – choose one problem, find the cause, design a small change.
**Do** – try it on a small scale (one shift, one route).
**Act** – if it works, make it the standard; if not, plan again.

blocks.p: **Lean** means removing **waste**: anything that uses time or money but adds no value for the customer. The 8 wastes (remember **TIMWOODS**):

head: Waste
Logistics example
rows: Moving pallets twice inside the warehouse
Pickers walking far for fast-moving items
Trucks waiting at the dock; customers waiting for answers
Picking orders hours before the truck is ready
Checking the same order three times
Wrong items, damaged goods, wrong labels
Not asking frontline staff for their ideas

blocks.p: A **kaizen event** brings a small team (including frontline staff) together for 1–3 days to improve one process quickly.
**5 Whys** – ask “why?” until you reach the real cause.

steps: Why was the delivery late? The truck left 45 minutes late.
Why? The evening shift was short of pickers.
Why? A big customer’s orders were moved to the evening.
Why? Nobody checked staff numbers when the schedule changed. → **Root cause: no check of capacity when schedules change.**

blocks.p: **Fishbone (Ishikawa) diagram** – list possible causes under headings such as **People, Methods, Machines, Materials, Measurement and Environment**, then test the most likely ones with data.

callout.title: Case: OTIF falls from 96% to 91%
callout.text: A food distributor finds three causes: new evening staff without full training, too many orders in the evening wave, and an untested billing system change. Fixes: mentors for new staff, two more pickers and one customer moved to the morning, and a check before invoices go out. After two weeks: picking accuracy 92% → 98%, trucks on time again, invoice errors below 2%.

terms.meaning: Making products before orders arrive and selling from stock.
Starting production only after a customer order.
Keeping parts in stock and assembling when an order comes.
terms.example: A laptop built with the chosen options.

terms.meaning: Materials Requirements Planning: turning the production plan and BOM into dated part orders.
On Time, In Full: the share of orders delivered on time and complete.
The share of orders delivered with no errors.
terms.example: 97.6% of orders had no wrong items or labels.

terms.meaning: An order that is on time, complete, undamaged and with correct documents.
Net Promoter Score: % promoters minus % detractors.
Plan, Do, Check, Act: a cycle for testing and standardising improvements.
terms.example: Test batch picking on one shift first.

terms.meaning: A way of working that removes waste and adds value for the customer.
terms.example: Moving fast movers close to packing.

terms.meaning: Any activity that uses resources but adds no value.
Continuous improvement in small steps, often in short team events.
terms.example: A two-day event to speed up receiving.

terms.meaning: Asking “why?” several times to find the root cause.
terms.example: Late truck → picking late → staff short → …

terms.meaning: A diagram that groups possible causes of a problem (also called Ishikawa).
terms.example: People, Methods, Machines, Materials, Measurement, Environment.

terms.meaning: The real reason a problem happens, not the symptom.
terms.example: No capacity check when schedules change.

quiz.q: A factory makes special cranes designed for each port customer. Which strategy is this?
quiz.why: Each crane is designed and made for one customer: engineer-to-order.

quiz.q: You plan 300 tables. Each needs 4 legs. You have 400 legs in stock. How many legs does MRP tell you to order?
500 orders: 480 on time, 470 in full, 455 on time AND in full. What is OTIF?
An order arrives on time and complete, but the invoice is wrong. Which quality dimension failed?
quiz.why: The documents did not match what was delivered: an information failure.

quiz.q: 70 promoters, 20 passives, 10 detractors out of 100 answers. What is the NPS?
What is the correct order of the PDCA cycle?
Pickers walk across the warehouse many times to collect fast-moving items. Which Lean waste is this?
quiz.why: Unnecessary movement of people is motion waste.

quiz.q: Which tool groups possible causes under headings like People, Methods and Machines?
quiz.why: The fishbone (Ishikawa) diagram organises possible causes.

quiz.q: Why should KPI definitions be written down exactly?
options: So that poor performance cannot hide behind a loose definition
quiz.why: For example, measuring ‘on time’ at dispatch instead of at delivery can make results look better than they are.

quiz.q: A new process works well in a two-week test. What is the ‘Act’ step?
options: Make it the standard way of working and train everyone
quiz.why: If the change works, standardise it so the improvement lasts.

questions.prompt: Name one product in Qatar for each strategy: make-to-stock, assemble-to-order and make-to-order. Explain why each strategy fits.
questions.hint: Think about how much the customer can change the product.

questions.prompt: A distributor delivered 800 orders last month: 760 on time, 752 complete, 736 on time and complete, 20 with documentation errors. Calculate OTIF and order accuracy. What would you look at first?
questions.hint: Order accuracy = orders with no errors ÷ all orders.

questions.prompt: Find three Lean wastes in a workplace you know (or a supermarket you visit). Name the waste type and suggest one fix for each.
Customers complain that deliveries arrive with damaged boxes. Use the 5 Whys to reach a possible root cause.
questions.hint: Write five questions and five answers.

questions.prompt: Plan a PDCA cycle to reduce picking errors from 2% to 0.5%. Write one or two sentences for each step.
Why can a high OTIF still come with unhappy customers?
One thing that is still not clear:
How confident are you with today's topic?
